title: The Yellow House on the Corner
description: The Yellow House on the Corner (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1980) is Rita Dove's first collection, published when she was twenty-seven. The Norton prints 'Geometry' from it, dated 1980, and the record covers the volume rather than the single poem because the anthology's selections are drawn from across its sections.
plot_or_argument: Dove's first book is unusually accomplished, and its distinguishing feature is the range of voices it takes on. The Akron poems are precise about place and class - a family in the industrial Midwest, a father's work, a house with a chimney - while 'This Life' lets Dove write in the first person of people she is not, from a nineteenth-century doctor to mythological women. 'Geometry' states the collection's aesthetic in miniature: the poem is interested in the forms that contain experience, in symmetry and the breaking of it, and in the moment when a pattern becomes visible. The book's title image, a yellow house on a corner, holds the two sides together, since a house is both a particular family's dwelling and a figure for the order the poems are making. Dove has said that the collection was written in the workshop years and that she was learning to use form to control feeling; what is striking on rereading is how little of it reads as apprentice work, and how much of her later manner - the sequence, the persona, the formal turn - is already present.
narrative_structure: Three sections of short lyrics and one sequence of persona poems; the volume moves from domestic and autobiographical poems to historical voices and back, and 'Geometry' is a single short lyric rather than a sequence.
meter_and_prosody: Metrically controlled free verse with frequent rhyme and near-rhyme; short lines and short poems; a diction that moves between the colloquial and the formal; and an image-based logic that prefers the shaped object to the statement.
historical_context: The book was published by Carnegie Mellon University Press in 1980, when Dove was teaching at Arizona State University after her Iowa MFA; it appeared in the same year as her second collection was in preparation, which is why the two are often discussed together. The late 1970s were the years in which a generation of Black poets born after the war - Dove, Komunyakaa, Yusef and others - began publishing first books that were neither Black Arts nor confessional.
literary_significance: The volume is Dove's debut and the source of the earliest poem the Norton prints; 'Geometry' is among the most anthologised of her short lyrics and is often used to introduce her formal control. The record is one of the two that answer the anthology's three Adolescence rows, since those poems come from the same period of her work.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1980. The Norton prints 'Geometry' from it. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is family and the ordinary life of a Black family in Akron, treated without sociology. The second is the making of art out of that material, since 'Geometry' is a poem about form itself. The third is history, which enters through the persona poems. The fourth is childhood and the gaining of a self-consciousness that the poems both record and resist.
summary: The book is in three sections and moves between the domestic and the historical. Its poems include portraits of family members in Akron, poems about childhood and the body, and a sequence, 'This Life', in which Dove speaks in the voices of historical and mythological figures. 'Geometry' - the poem the Norton prints - is a short lyric about order, measurement and the shapes a life is fitted into, and it shows the formal preoccupations that run through the volume.
critical_context: Criticism treats the first book as the foundation of Dove's manner and notes that its persona poems anticipate Mother Love; the standard account of her development places the Akron poems and the 'This Life' sequence as the two poles between which her later work moves. 'Geometry' is usually discussed for its treatment of form as a subject.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its table of contents and on the published accounts of Dove's early work. The first printing of the anthology's three Adolescence poems was not verified and is not asserted here.

title: Museum
description: Museum (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1983) is Rita Dove's second collection, and it is the one in which she began to write about Europe, art and the position of the observer. The Norton prints 'Parsley' and 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' from it.
plot_or_argument: Museum is Dove's argument with the museum as a way of seeing, and its two selections state both sides of the argument. 'Parsley' takes a historical atrocity and refuses to let it be contemplated from a distance: the poem moves between the general's voice, the soldiers' and the victims', and its repetitions of 'perejil' make the massacre happen in language rather than behind it. The poem's form - four numbered sections, a chorus of cane-cutters, a dictator's aria - is operatic, and its ambition is to do in lyric what a documentary cannot, which is to show how a word becomes an instrument of murder. 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' is the counterweight: a short, first-person refusal of the position of the museum visitor, of the aesthetic appreciation that turns suffering into an exhibit. Read together, the two poems define the book's subject as the ethics of looking, which is the same subject Dove would return to in the persona poems of Mother Love and in Sonata Mulattica.
narrative_structure: A collection of short lyrics and one long four-part narrative poem, arranged so that the museum poems and the history poems alternate; 'Parsley' is the volume's structural centre.
meter_and_prosody: Controlled free verse with rhyme and repetition; multiple voices inside a single poem; a plain, declarative line for the historical passages; and an imagery of paintings, mirrors and windows throughout.
historical_context: Museum appeared in 1983, the year before Dove began teaching at Arizona State, and it was written in part during and after her Fulbright year in Germany; its European poems come from that period, and 'Parsley' was researched from accounts of the 1937 massacre, in which Trujillo's soldiers killed an estimated 20,000 Haitians along the border. The poem's attention to the shibboleth of 'perejil' comes from the historical record.
literary_significance: 'Parsley' is Dove's most ambitious early poem and one of the most important American poems of the 1980s about state violence; it is a standard anthology piece and a Norton selection. With 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' it shows the anthology representing Dove's historical range as well as her domestic lyrics.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1983. The Norton prints 'Parsley' and 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the museum and the gaze, and the book's title names the institution it is arguing with. The second is the history of racial violence, above all in 'Parsley'. The third is the artist's relation to European culture, which Dove approaches as a Black American visitor rather than as an heir. The fourth is the refusal of contemplation, which is an aesthetic as well as a moral position.
summary: The collection moves between poems written out of travel in Europe - museums, paintings, cathedrals, the Mediterranean - and poems about American history and the body, and its central poem is 'Parsley', a long narrative lyric about the 1937 massacre of Haitian cane-cutters in the Dominican Republic on the orders of Rafael Trujillo. That poem's device is the dictator's inability to pronounce the Spanish word for parsley, 'perejil', which was used to identify Haitians by their accent, and Dove builds a four-part poem around the word and the killing. 'Poem in Which I Refuse Contemplation' is a short lyric about refusing the aesthetic distance that museums teach.
critical_context: Criticism reads 'Parsley' as a landmark of the American historical lyric and discusses its operatic structure and its use of the shibboleth; the ethics of Dove's multiple voicing - whether a non-Haitian poet can speak the victims' chorus - has been debated. Museum as a whole is usually treated as the book in which Dove's interest in art and history became explicit.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description of 'Parsley' rests on its published text and the poem's standard critical accounts, and the casualty figure is given as the historical estimates give it, not as the poem states it.

title: Thomas and Beulah
description: Thomas and Beulah (Pittsburgh: Carnegie Mellon University Press, 1986) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1987. It is a book-length sequence in two halves, telling the lives of Dove's maternal grandparents - Thomas, who came north from Tennessee to work in Akron, and Beulah, who married him - and the Norton prints three of its poems: 'The Event', 'The Zeppelin Factory' and 'Dusting'.
plot_or_argument: The book's achievement is to give two ordinary lives the scale of history without inflating them. Dove works in short lyrics arranged in sequence, and the sequence does the work that prose would do: the reader assembles a marriage out of moments, and the gaps between poems are as significant as the poems. Thomas's half is full of the world - the Great Migration, the war, the zeppelin works, the race riot of 1919 in Akron and the labour organising of the 1930s - while Beulah's half is full of the house, and the asymmetry is the book's argument about the different freedoms of men and women in the same life. The poems are in the third person and refuse the poet's commentary; Dove does not tell the reader what her grandparents' lives mean, and the sequence's last poems, in which Beulah is dying among her daughters, are remarkable for their calm. The title's two names give the book its form: it is a double portrait, and the two halves are not equal in the amount of the world they can reach. The Pulitzer made Dove, at thirty-four, the second African American poet to win it, and the book has become the standard model for the American book-length family sequence. Its most important technical decision is that neither half narrates its own meaning: the reader is given the objects - a mandolin, a lemon tree, a zeppelin, a dust cloth - and left to assemble the lives from them, which is why the sequence rewards reading in order rather than in excerpts.
narrative_structure: Two halves of about twenty-five short poems each, in chronological order within each half, with the two lives running in parallel rather than interleaved; the poems are short lyrics, many of a single stanza, and no poem comments on another.
meter_and_prosody: Third-person lyrics in controlled free verse with rhyme; plain diction and domestic objects; the historical world admitted through names, machines and dates rather than through statement; and an absence of the poet's 'I'.
historical_context: The book appeared in 1986 from Carnegie Mellon and won the Pulitzer in 1987, the year of Toni Morrison's Beloved and of a wider public argument about African American family history; Dove's grandparents had migrated from Tennessee to Akron, and the Goodyear Tire & Rubber Company, where Thomas worked and where Dove's father became the company's first Black chemist, is the book's industrial ground.
literary_significance: Thomas and Beulah is one of the most honoured American poetry books of the 1980s and is the work for which Dove is best known; its model of the documentary family sequence has been widely imitated, and the Norton's three selections from it give the anthology the book's scale as well as its individual lyrics. With the three Adolescence poems and four other lyrics, Dove has ten selections in the period, more than any other poet.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Carnegie Mellon University Press (Pittsburgh) in 1986; Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, 1987. The Norton prints 'The Event', 'The Zeppelin Factory' and 'Dusting'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Great Migration, since Thomas's journey north is the book's historical engine. The second is marriage and its asymmetry, which the two-part structure embodies. The third is labour, both industrial and domestic, and the way it shapes a body. The fourth is memory and inheritance, since the poet is reconstructing lives she knows only through family story.
summary: The first half, 'Mandolin', follows Thomas from his arrival in Akron and the death of his friend Lem, through courtship, marriage, the birth of four daughters and his work at the Goodyear factory, to the lemons he grows in old age. The second half, 'Canary in Bloom', follows Beulah from her marriage through the household, her illness, her widowhood and her death. 'The Event' is one of the poems of Thomas's early life, 'The Zeppelin Factory' recalls the airship works in Akron and the men who worked in it, and 'Dusting' is a short poem of Beulah's domestic life.
critical_context: Criticism reads the sequence as a recovery of Black family history in the Great Migration and discusses its refusal of the poet's voice, its use of the two-part structure to mark gender difference, and its handling of the 1919 Akron riot and the zeppelin works. The Pulitzer is usually treated as the moment Dove became a public poet, and the book as the model for the documentary sequences of the 1990s.
research_notes: The sequence was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its published structure and on the standard critical accounts, and the placement of the three printed poems in their halves is given from the sequence's contents. Internal dates such as the 1919 Akron riot are given as the historical record, not as the poems' own statements.

title: The Business of Fancydancing
description: The Business of Fancydancing: Stories and Poems (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992) is Sherman Alexie's first book, published when he was twenty-five. It mixes short stories and poems without marking the boundary, and the Norton prints 'Pawn Shop' from it.
plot_or_argument: The book's formal oddity is its refusal to separate poetry from prose, and that refusal is its argument: on the reservation, a story and a poem are the same act, and the distinction belongs to the publisher. Alexie's early voice is direct, funny and wounded, and it uses the materials of late-twentieth-century American popular culture - basketball, television, beer, cars - as if they were a literary inheritance, which for his characters they are. 'Pawn Shop' shows the method in miniature: a flat, reportorial prose that lists what is being exchanged and what it costs, and a refusal to explain the transaction's meaning. The book's politics are inseparable from its comedy, since the jokes are about the conditions the poems are also mourning, and the title's irony - that Indian identity is a business - is the collection's central insight. Its publication by Hanging Loose, a small Brooklyn press, placed Alexie outside the university and the Native American studies circuit, and its success made him the most visible Native writer of his generation while he was still in his twenties.
narrative_structure: A collection of short lyrics, prose poems and short stories in roughly chronological arrangement by the age of the speaker, with no section headings separating the genres.
literary_form: Collection of poems and short stories (debut volume)
meter_and_prosody: Short lines and very short paragraphs; a demotic, joke-timed voice; brand names and basketball as common reference; repetition and a deliberate flatness at moments of grief; and no figurative heightening.
historical_context: Hanging Loose Press published the book in 1992, the year Alexie graduated from Washington State University, and it appeared in the same season as The Lone Ranger and Tonto Fistfight in Heaven (1993), which followed within a year. The early 1990s were the years of the Native American literary boom created by the successes of Momaday, Silko, Erdrich and Welch, and Alexie's debut was read as the arrival of an urban, pop-culture Indian voice.
literary_significance: The book is the debut of the most widely read Native American writer of his generation and the source of one of the Norton's four Alexie selections; it establishes the mixed-genre form he would keep, and 'Pawn Shop' is a standard example of his prose poem. The Norton list carried 'Pawn Shop' as undated before this wave; this record fixes it at 1992.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Hanging Loose Press (Brooklyn) in 1992. The Norton prints 'Pawn Shop'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is reservation life and its economies, both the pawn shop and the powwow. The second is alcoholism and loss, which the book treats without moralising. The third is the performance of Indianness for white expectations, which the title names. The fourth is family and the inheritance of damage, carried in the book's short, unexplained scenes.
summary: The book's seventy-odd pieces are set on and around the Spokane reservation and move between first-person lyrics, prose poems and very short stories. Its subjects are drinking, basketball, family violence, the deaths of friends and the business of being an Indian in front of white readers - the title's 'fancydancing' is both the powwow dance and the performance of identity for an audience. 'Pawn Shop' is one of its prose pieces, a single-paragraph narrative about the commerce of the reservation town.
critical_context: Criticism reads the debut as a departure from the ceremonial mode of the Native American Renaissance, noting its demotic voice and its refusal of anthropological explanation; the standard account of Alexie's career treats the first book as the source of the tone he developed in the stories and films.
research_notes: The collection was not read in full for this record; the description rests on its published contents and on the standard accounts of Alexie's early work. The 1992 date fixes the Norton list's undated row.

title: The Summer of Black Widows
description: The Summer of Black Widows (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1996) is Sherman Alexie's second collection of poems, published in the year of his novel Indian Killer. The Norton prints 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' from its third sequence, a group of poems about the death of his sister in a house fire.
plot_or_argument: The collection shows Alexie working in received forms - the villanelle, the sestina - while keeping his demotic voice, and 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is the clearest example: a villanelle's two refrains are made to do the work of grief, so that the form's repetition becomes the obsessive return of the mourner. The sequence it closes moves from the fire itself through the family's aftermath to the brother's guilt at having survived and at having made art from the death, and the last poem's formal control is the point - the discipline is what the grief is being held in. Alexie's habit of undercutting solemnity with a joke is present even here, which makes the poem harder rather than easier. The collection as a whole is more various than the debut: it includes love poems, a long poem about basketball and a sequence on the Spokane world, and its range is what the Norton's selection represents, a poet who can write a villanelle about his sister and a joke about Crazy Horse in the same book.
narrative_structure: A collection of sequences, with the sister poems forming the third and the villanelle placed last in it; the poems are short and the sequences are held together by recurring images rather than narrative.
meter_and_prosody: Demotic free verse with formal poems set among it; a villanelle with two refrains; jokes inside elegies; and a line that is closer to speech than to song.
historical_context: The collection appeared in 1996, the year of Indian Killer, and belongs to the period in which Alexie was publishing a book a year; Hanging Loose had published his debut and remained his publisher for poetry. His sister's death in a house fire is the biographical ground of the sequence, and the poems are unusual among his work for their directness about family loss.
literary_significance: The collection contains Alexie's most formally accomplished poem and is the source of the Norton's third poem selection; 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is regularly cited in discussions of the villanelle in contemporary American poetry, which is a surprising place to find a Spokane writer and exactly the point. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave; this record fixes it at 1996.
bibliographical_notes: First published by Hanging Loose Press (Brooklyn) in 1996. The Norton prints 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke'. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the death of a sibling and the guilt of the survivor, which the sequence treats without consolation. The second is the relation of art to grief, since the brother is a writer and the poem knows it. The third is family and the reservation world in which the loss happens. The fourth is form itself, since the villanelle's refrains make repetition a figure for mourning.
summary: The book is in several sequences and mixes love poems, political poems, poems about basketball and a long central sequence about the death of Alexie's sister. 'Sister Fire, Brother Smoke' is a villanelle, the last poem of that sequence, in which the brother mourns the sister and confronts his own survival; the poem's repeated lines carry both the fire and the smoke that is left of the person.
critical_context: Criticism notes Alexie's use of received forms as a claim on the tradition and discusses the sister sequence as his most direct treatment of grief; the standard account of the collection reads it as the book in which he proved he was a poet as well as a storyteller.
research_notes: The collection's date is confirmed from its publication record; the individual poems' first periodical appearances were not traced. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave.

title: At Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School
description: 'At Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School' is a poem from The Business of Fancydancing (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992), Alexie's first book. It is about a photograph of students at an Indian boarding school, and it is the most directly historical poem in his debut.
plot_or_argument: The poem's method is ekphrasis as indictment: the photograph is treated as a document and as a lie at the same time, since the order and cleanliness of the line-up are exactly what the school was for. Alexie's short lines let him place a fact beside an image without arguing, and the poem's power comes from the reader's knowledge of what the boarding schools did - the cutting of hair, the prohibition of Native languages, the separation of children from parents, the motto 'kill the Indian, save the man'. The poem does not supply that history, and its refusal to explain is a refusal to make the children into a lesson. It is also one of the earliest poems in which Alexie writes about photography, a subject he returns to throughout his work, and its treatment of the camera as an instrument of both record and violence is characteristic of the Native American writing of the period, which had begun to read the photographic archive against itself.
narrative_structure: A short free-verse poem in brief lines, organised as a reading of a single photograph with no stanza division and no narrative development.
meter_and_prosody: Short unpunctuated lines; present tense; a flat descriptive tone that refuses outrage; and an absence of simile, so that the photograph stays a photograph.
historical_context: The Business of Fancydancing appeared in 1992, and the poem belongs to the period of public reckoning with the boarding-school system that would produce the 2000s scholarship on it; Navajo Monument Valley Tribal School is a school on the Navajo Nation, and the poem's title names a specific institution rather than a generic one.
literary_significance: The poem is the historical centre of Alexie's debut and the one most often taught in courses on boarding-school literature; it is a Norton selection, and the list carried it as undated before this wave.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Business of Fancydancing (Brooklyn: Hanging Loose Press, 1992). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The first subject is the Indian boarding school and the assimilation policy it served. The second is the photograph as a document that records and conceals at once. The third is the survival of the children in the picture, which the poem insists on without sentiment. The fourth is language, since the schools' central act was to forbid it.
summary: The poem describes a photograph of Navajo children lined up at a tribal school, and it reads the image for what it does not show: the children's names, the languages they were forbidden, the families they were taken from. It moves between the photograph's flat surface and the history the surface holds down, and its short lines keep the poem close to the picture rather than letting it escape into statement.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem with the photographic archive of the boarding schools and treats its refusal to narrate as its ethical choice; the standard account of Alexie's early work places it among the poems that carry the book's historical weight.
research_notes: The collection's date is confirmed from its publication record; the poem's first periodical appearance was not traced. The Norton list carried the poem as undated before this wave.
